sources.title: Apple says it’s tightening macOS ‘Full Disk Access’ controls due to new risks from AI agents - TechCrunch
passages: Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS.
The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said.
This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history.
We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote.
The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages.
Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change.
AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings.

extraction.body: Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS. The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said. Apple’s statement comes shortly after Inc. columnist Jason Aten reported that Muse knew the content of his private messages — even though he claimed to have not given the AI agent permission. The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages. The decision to limit the Mac feature also comes after a Wired report cited that a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data. AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings. In Muse’s case, the AI optionally allows users to enable Full Disk Access. This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history. “Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems…without users’ full knowledge and understanding,” Apple said in a new blog post aimed at developers. The company says that, going forward, it will introduce new controls aimed at ensuring that users who “genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access” can do so only with “very explicit user action.” “Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote. Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change. passages: Apple will add new limits for “full disk access” on Mac in response to risks posed by AI agents, as reported earlier by TechCrunch.

In an update on Friday, Apple says it’s rolling out new controls to “ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.” The change comes just weeks after Inc’s Jason Aten found that Meta’s Muse AI somehow knew the contents of his messages, despite not giving the chatbot explicit permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac.
Apple didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

In an update on Friday, Apple says it’s rolling out new controls to “ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.” The change comes just weeks after Inc’s Jason Aten found that Meta’s Muse AI somehow knew the contents of his messages, despite not giving the chatbot explicit permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone pushed back on this report, saying access to Messages is “entirely opt-in.” Stone added that you have to “enable both Full Disk Access and the Messages connector for Muse to be able to read your Messages content.” Now Apple is addressing how developers use that sweeping access, saying: > Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users’ full knowledge and understanding… As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. Full disk access is a permission on macOS that gives an app access to a user’s entire system. Apple says the feature “largely sidesteps” privacy controls offered to users “to allow backup apps to function properly on Mac.” The company doesn’t say when it plans to roll out its update for full disk access. Apple didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

extraction.body: Apple is making it harder for apps to get sweeping access to a Mac. The company said on Friday that it will add new controls to the Full Disk Access setting in macOS, so users can grant it only through "very explicit user action".Full Disk Access lets an app read almost everything on a Mac, from files and mail to messages and browsing history. In a post on its developer website, Apple said the setting exists so backup apps can work properly, and that it largely bypasses the privacy controls built into macOS. "Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk," Apple wrote, adding that this happens without users' "full knowledge and understanding".Apple also flagged a less obvious concern. When a communication app gets this access, the privacy of the people a user is chatting with is exposed as well.The company has not explained how the new controls will work or when they will arrive, and it did not name any app or developer. It did point to AI agents, though, warning that the risks of this level of access "will grow substantially" as agents become more capable and autonomous.AI agents on the Mac now routinely ask for full system accessThe announcement follows a claim by US columnist Jason Aten that Meta's Muse AI agent read private messages on his Mac mini without his permission. Andy Stone, Meta's vice president of communications, said on X that Muse can read Messages only if users enable both Full Disk Access and its Messages connector, and that access can be revoked anytime.Muse is not the only agent asking for this. In August, OpenAI added an opt-in feature to its ChatGPT Mac app that reads, summarises and sends texts for users, and it also needs Full Disk Access. OpenAI says more than 35 million people now use its agent tools, ChatGPT Work and Codex, up from 10 million in July.Full Disk Access is staying on macOS. Apple's aim is to make sure anyone handing an AI agent that much control knows what they are signing off on.You use AI every day.

sources.title: Apple Locks Down Mac Disk Access as AI Agents Pose New Risks
passages: Apple just threw up new security barriers around Mac computers, responding to what the company calls 'substantial' risks from AI agents that can dig through user files without explicit permission.
Apple's preemptive security move signals a broader industry awakening to the unique risks posed by AI agents.
The company announced Friday it's rolling out new restrictions for 'full disk access' permissions, a powerful capability that lets apps read virtually everything on a user's computer.
The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions.

According to Apple's developer update, the changes aim to 'ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.' The timing isn't coincidental.

extraction.body: Apple just threw up new security barriers around Mac computers, responding to what the company calls 'substantial' risks from AI agents that can dig through user files without explicit permission. The move comes weeks after a troubling incident where Meta's Muse AI appeared to access private messages without clear user consent, highlighting how AI tools are pushing the boundaries of data access in ways that weren't anticipated. Apple is slamming the brakes on how deeply apps can dig into Mac file systems, and AI agents are the reason why. The company announced Friday it's rolling out new restrictions for 'full disk access' permissions, a powerful capability that lets apps read virtually everything on a user's computer. According to Apple's developer update, the changes aim to 'ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.' The timing isn't coincidental. Just weeks ago, Inc's Jason Aten discovered that Meta's Muse AI chatbot somehow knew the contents of his private messages, despite never explicitly granting the tool permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac. The incident, first reported by The Verge, sent ripples through the tech community as it highlighted a troubling gap between user expectations and AI capabilities. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone quickly pushed back, insisting that access to Messages is 'entirely opt-in' and that users must explicitly grant permission. But the controversy exposed how AI agents - sophisticated tools that can autonomously navigate systems and perform tasks - operate in ways that traditional app permission models weren't designed to handle. Unlike conventional software that follows predictable paths, AI agents can dynamically explore file systems, connect disparate data points, and infer information from seemingly unrelated sources. This creates what security experts call 'permission creep' - where an AI tool granted basic access can leverage that foothold to gather far more information than users intended. Apple's response reflects the company's broader privacy-first philosophy, but it also signals recognition that existing security frameworks are struggling to keep pace with AI development. The new controls will likely require apps to implement more granular permission requests, forcing developers to be explicit about what data their AI tools actually need. But it also means greater control over what these increasingly sophisticated tools can access. The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions. Microsoft Windows and various Linux distributions use similar 'administrator' or 'root' access models that could face the same AI-related vulnerabilities. Google's Chrome OS, with its more restrictive app sandbox approach, may prove more resilient, but even Google will need to consider how AI agents interact with cloud-based file systems. Industry observers expect this to be the first of many security updates as companies grapple with AI tools that blur the line between user intent and automated action. As AI agents become more sophisticated and autonomous, the traditional model of granting broad permissions upfront may prove inadequate. Apple's preemptive security move signals a broader industry awakening to the unique risks posed by AI agents. As these tools become more autonomous and capable of connecting data in unexpected ways, traditional permission models are proving inadequate. The real test will be whether other platform makers follow suit quickly enough, and whether developers can build AI tools that are both powerful and respectful of user boundaries. For now, Mac users can expect more security prompts but also more control over their digital privacy.

extraction.body: Apple just threw up new security barriers around Mac computers, responding to what the company calls 'substantial' risks from AI agents that can dig through user files without explicit permission. The move comes weeks after a troubling incident where Meta's Muse AI appeared to access private messages without clear user consent, highlighting how AI tools are pushing the boundaries of data access in ways that weren't anticipated. Apple is slamming the brakes on how deeply apps can dig into Mac file systems, and AI agents are the reason why. The company announced Friday it's rolling out new restrictions for 'full disk access' permissions, a powerful capability that lets apps read virtually everything on a user's computer. According to Apple's developer update, the changes aim to 'ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.' The timing isn't coincidental. Just weeks ago, Inc's Jason Aten discovered that Meta's Muse AI chatbot somehow knew the contents of his private messages, despite never explicitly granting the tool permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac. The incident, first reported by The Verge, sent ripples through the tech community as it highlighted a troubling gap between user expectations and AI capabilities. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone quickly pushed back, insisting that access to Messages is 'entirely opt-in' and that users must explicitly grant permission. But the controversy exposed how AI agents - sophisticated tools that can autonomously navigate systems and perform tasks - operate in ways that traditional app permission models weren't designed to handle. Unlike conventional software that follows predictable paths, AI agents can dynamically explore file systems, connect disparate data points, and infer information from seemingly unrelated sources. This creates what security experts call 'permission creep' - where an AI tool granted basic access can leverage that foothold to gather far more information than users intended. Apple's response reflects the company's broader privacy-first philosophy, but it also signals recognition that existing security frameworks are struggling to keep pace with AI development. The new controls will likely require apps to implement more granular permission requests, forcing developers to be explicit about what data their AI tools actually need. But it also means greater control over what these increasingly sophisticated tools can access. The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions. Microsoft Windows and various Linux distributions use similar 'administrator' or 'root' access models that could face the same AI-related vulnerabilities. Google's Chrome OS, with its more restrictive app sandbox approach, may prove more resilient, but even Google will need to consider how AI agents interact with cloud-based file systems. Industry observers expect this to be the first of many security updates as companies grapple with AI tools that blur the line between user intent and automated action. As AI agents become more sophisticated and autonomous, the traditional model of granting broad permissions upfront may prove inadequate. extraction.body: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is reviewing an issue in updated flight management computer (FMC) software on some Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. Two U.S. airlines have told Boeing they will not accept new aircraft carrying the software, and the review comes as Boeing awaits certification of the 737-10. In a statement to Airways, the FAA said it is aware of a potential issue in a software update for the flight computers on certain 737 MAX aircraft and is working closely with Boeing and the airlines. The agency said it "will convene a Corrective Action Review Board (CARB) and will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern." According to the FAA, a CARB consists of FAA safety experts and is the agency's standard process for determining whether an issue is a safety concern and, if so, how to address it most effectively. Boeing told operators in a bulletin in late August that the glitch is not an immediate safety issue , CBS reported. In a statement to Airways, a Boeing spokesperson said the company informed all 737 operators last month "about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario" and "shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases." The spokesperson said Boeing's engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue. The Wall Street Journal first reported the problem. CBS reported that the condition can arise in rare cases when the crew is flying a precision approach with the autopilot engaged, initiates a missed approach, or go-around, and then changes the preprogrammed flight plan. In that situation, the flight guidance system may incorrectly transition out of vertical navigation (VNAV) to a simpler pitch mode such as level change or vertical speed, according to Boeing's description of the problem reported by Aviation Week . VNAV follows the vertical profile the FMC computes from the flight plan's altitude and speed constraints. Level change instead holds a target airspeed while the autothrottle sets climb or idle thrust, and vertical speed holds a rate of climb or descent the pilot selects. Neither mode follows the FMC's vertical path, so crews must manage those constraints themselves. CBS noted the scenario would typically occur close to the airport, where crew workload is already high, and Boeing said pilots must take additional steps to use automated guidance on the next approach. Boeing said the autopilot continues to function if VNAV disengages and that pilots are trained to land without it. The company told CNBC it is "working directly with airlines to formalize a procedure that will allow pilots to reenable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur." Boeing told Airways it "anticipates the next software update in 2028" and is working to accelerate that timeline based on operator feedback. CBS reported that Boeing's initial bulletin also said updated pilot guidance would follow in November, and that Boeing is working to bring both forward. The glitch surfaced in FMC software versions 14 and 14.1, CBS reported. Alaska Airlines (AS), American Airlines (AA), Southwest Airlines (WN), and United Airlines (UA) each told CBS that none of their in-service 737 MAX aircraft use the affected software. Southwest told CNBC that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes." Those statements concern aircraft already in service. For new deliveries, Southwest and United have told Boeing they will not accept delivery of new aircraft with the affected software and would take aircraft with a previous version instead, CBS reported. The fleet statements cover four U.S. carriers. CBS said it had also contacted Allegiant Air (G4), which operates the 737 MAX, for comment. Boeing told Airways it did not have specific aircraft figures to share, so it remains unclear how many undelivered aircraft carry versions 14 or 14.1, or whether any operator outside the U.S. already flies with them. An airline first told Boeing about the condition in November 2024, according to CBS. Boeing reviewed it and concluded in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue. Boeing received what a source described to CBS as "additional information from operators" earlier this year, which prompted it to launch a formal safety review board. The Wall Street Journal reported that the formal review began in September, according to an Investing.com summary of the newspaper's report . The board's findings went to the FAA this month and will be reviewed by the CARB. Boeing told Airways that it informed the FAA of the issue as part of its safety review process and is working under the agency's oversight to complete the software update. The FAA certified the 737-7 on August 3. CBS reported that the aircraft was certified with software version 14 and that Southwest, which accounts for nearly all of the type's order book, had been set to begin receiving it this fall; it is unclear whether the airline will take delivery now. CNBC reported it was not immediately clear whether the 737-7 could be delivered or flown with an older software version. The 737-10 used version 14.1 during its certification testing, according to CBS. Boeing completed the final planned certification flight in July, and Alaska Chief Operating Officer Jason Berry told Reuters on September 24 that the airline expected FAA certification by the end of September . Aviation Week reported that it remains unclear whether the software issue will affect the timing of either 737-7 deliveries or 737-10 certification. The FAA's statement did not address either program. Alaska said on September 26 that it has been engaged with Boeing and the FAA "and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps." Alaska holds an order for 105 737-10s and options for 35 more . In his September 24 interview, before the software issue was reported, Berry said Alaska expected its first aircraft in spring 2027 and passenger service between April and mid-May that year. He added that Alaska must complete certification work on the pilots' head-up display after the FAA approves the aircraft, a process he expected to take a "few months." The CARB will review Boeing's safety findings, and the FAA told Airways that the board will also review Boeing's proposed solution. Boeing told Airways it had no further information at this time on whether 737-7 deliveries can proceed with an earlier software load, whether the fix will require pilot training beyond a software update, or what additional operator information prompted its formal safety review. passages: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is reviewing an issue in updated flight management computer (FMC) software on some Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. Two U.S. airlines have told Boeing they will not accept new aircraft carrying the software, and the review comes as Boeing awaits certification of the 737-10.

In a statement to Airways, the FAA said it is aware of a potential issue in a software update for the flight computers on certain 737 MAX aircraft and is working closely with Boeing and the airlines. The agency said it "will convene a Corrective Action Review Board (CARB) and will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern." According to the FAA, a CARB consists of FAA safety experts and is the agency's standard process for determining whether an issue is a safety concern and, if so, how to address it most effectively.

Boeing told operators in a bulletin in late August that the glitch is not an immediate safety issue , CBS reported. In a statement to Airways, a Boeing spokesperson said the company informed all 737 operators last month "about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario" and "shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases." The spokesperson said Boeing's engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue. The Wall Street Journal first reported the problem.

CBS reported that the condition can arise in rare cases when the crew is flying a precision approach with the autopilot engaged, initiates a missed approach, or go-around, and then changes the preprogrammed flight plan. In that situation, the flight guidance system may incorrectly transition out of vertical navigation (VNAV) to a simpler pitch mode such as level change or vertical speed, according to Boeing's description of the problem reported by Aviation Week .

VNAV follows the vertical profile the FMC computes from the flight plan's altitude and speed constraints. Level change instead holds a target airspeed while the autothrottle sets climb or idle thrust, and vertical speed holds a rate of climb or descent the pilot selects. Neither mode follows the FMC's vertical path, so crews must manage those constraints themselves. CBS noted the scenario would typically occur close to the airport, where crew workload is already high, and Boeing said pilots must take additional steps to use automated guidance on the next approach.

Boeing said the autopilot continues to function if VNAV disengages and that pilots are trained to land without it. The company told CNBC it is "working directly with airlines to formalize a procedure that will allow pilots to reenable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur." Boeing told Airways it "anticipates the next software update in 2028" and is working to accelerate that timeline based on operator feedback. CBS reported that Boeing's initial bulletin also said updated pilot guidance would follow in November, and that Boeing is working to bring both forward.

The glitch surfaced in FMC software versions 14 and 14.1, CBS reported. Alaska Airlines (AS), American Airlines (AA), Southwest Airlines (WN), and United Airlines (UA) each told CBS that none of their in-service 737 MAX aircraft use the affected software. Southwest told CNBC that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes."

Those statements concern aircraft already in service. For new deliveries, Southwest and United have told Boeing they will not accept delivery of new aircraft with the affected software and would take aircraft with a previous version instead, CBS reported.

The fleet statements cover four U.S. carriers. CBS said it had also contacted Allegiant Air (G4), which operates the 737 MAX, for comment. Boeing told Airways it did not have specific aircraft figures to share, so it remains unclear how many undelivered aircraft carry versions 14 or 14.1, or whether any operator outside the U.S. already flies with them.
An airline first told Boeing about the condition in November 2024, according to CBS. Boeing reviewed it and concluded in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue.

Boeing received what a source described to CBS as "additional information from operators" earlier this year, which prompted it to launch a formal safety review board. The Wall Street Journal reported that the formal review began in September, according to an Investing.com summary of the newspaper's report . The board's findings went to the FAA this month and will be reviewed by the CARB. Boeing told Airways that it informed the FAA of the issue as part of its safety review process and is working under the agency's oversight to complete the software update.

The FAA certified the 737-7 on August 3. CBS reported that the aircraft was certified with software version 14 and that Southwest, which accounts for nearly all of the type's order book, had been set to begin receiving it this fall; it is unclear whether the airline will take delivery now. CNBC reported it was not immediately clear whether the 737-7 could be delivered or flown with an older software version.

The 737-10 used version 14.1 during its certification testing, according to CBS. Boeing completed the final planned certification flight in July, and Alaska Chief Operating Officer Jason Berry told Reuters on September 24 that the airline expected FAA certification by the end of September .

Aviation Week reported that it remains unclear whether the software issue will affect the timing of either 737-7 deliveries or 737-10 certification. The FAA's statement did not address either program. Alaska said on September 26 that it has been engaged with Boeing and the FAA "and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps."

Alaska holds an order for 105 737-10s and options for 35 more . In his September 24 interview, before the software issue was reported, Berry said Alaska expected its first aircraft in spring 2027 and passenger service between April and mid-May that year. He added that Alaska must complete certification work on the pilots' head-up display after the FAA approves the aircraft, a process he expected to take a "few months."
The CARB will review Boeing's safety findings, and the FAA told Airways that the board will also review Boeing's proposed solution.

Boeing told Airways it had no further information at this time on whether 737-7 deliveries can proceed with an earlier software load, whether the fix will require pilot training beyond a software update, or what additional operator information prompted its formal safety review. The FAA's statement to Airways did not say whether the CARB must conclude before the agency certifies the 737-10.

Following a thorough review, a panel of FAA safety experts on Friday determined a software issue in certain Boeing 737 MAX flight computers is not a safety concern. The FAA’s Corrective Action Review Board made that determination because pilots retain full control of the aircraft and the indications to the flight crew are clear and unambiguous.
As with any situation, the FAA will consider appropriate action if it receives new information about this issue.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the problem.
The FAA's statement did not address either program.
Alaska said on September 26 that it has been engaged with Boeing and the FAA "and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps."

Boeing told Airways it had no further information at this time on whether 737-7 deliveries can proceed with an earlier software load, whether the fix will require pilot training beyond a software update, or what additional operator information prompted its formal safety review.

Alaska holds an order for 105 737-10s and options for 35 more .

He added that Alaska must complete certification work on the pilots' head-up display after the FAA approves the aircraft, a process he expected to take a "few months."
CBS reported that Boeing's initial bulletin also said updated pilot guidance would follow in November, and that Boeing is working to bring both forward.
The fleet statements cover four U.S. carriers.
CBS said it had also contacted Allegiant Air (G4), which operates the 737 MAX, for comment.
Southwest told CNBC that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes."

In that situation, the flight guidance system may incorrectly transition out of vertical navigation (VNAV) to a simpler pitch mode such as level change or vertical speed, according to Boeing's description of the problem reported by Aviation Week .
Boeing reviewed it and concluded in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue.

CBS noted the scenario would typically occur close to the airport, where crew workload is already high, and Boeing said pilots must take additional steps to use automated guidance on the next approach.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is reviewing an issue in updated flight management computer (FMC) software on some Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. Two U.S. airlines have told Boeing they will not accept new aircraft carrying the software, and the review comes as Boeing awaits certification of the 737-10. In a statement to Airways, the FAA said it is aware of a potential issue in a software update for the flight computers on certain 737 MAX aircraft and is working closely with Boeing and the airlines. The agency said it "will convene a Corrective Action Review Board (CARB) and will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern." According to the FAA, a CARB consists of FAA safety experts and is the agency's standard process for determining whether an issue is a safety concern and, if so, how to address it most effectively. Boeing told operators in a bulletin in late August that the glitch is not an immediate safety issue , CBS reported. In a statement to Airways, a Boeing spokesperson said the company informed all 737 operators last month "about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario" and "shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases." The spokesperson said Boeing's engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue. The Wall Street Journal first reported the problem. CBS reported that the condition can arise in rare cases when the crew is flying a precision approach with the autopilot engaged, initiates a missed approach, or go-around, and then changes the preprogrammed flight plan. In that situation, the flight guidance system may incorrectly transition out of vertical navigation (VNAV) to a simpler pitch mode such as level change or vertical speed, according to Boeing's description of the problem reported by Aviation Week . VNAV follows the vertical profile the FMC computes from the flight plan's altitude and speed constraints. Level change instead holds a target airspeed while the autothrottle sets climb or idle thrust, and vertical speed holds a rate of climb or descent the pilot selects. Neither mode follows the FMC's vertical path, so crews must manage those constraints themselves. CBS noted the scenario would typically occur close to the airport, where crew workload is already high, and Boeing said pilots must take additional steps to use automated guidance on the next approach. Boeing said the autopilot continues to function if VNAV disengages and that pilots are trained to land without it. The company told CNBC it is "working directly with airlines to formalize a procedure that will allow pilots to reenable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur." Boeing told Airways it "anticipates the next software update in 2028" and is working to accelerate that timeline based on operator feedback. CBS reported that Boeing's initial bulletin also said updated pilot guidance would follow in November, and that Boeing is working to bring both forward. The glitch surfaced in FMC software versions 14 and 14.1, CBS reported. Alaska Airlines (AS), American Airlines (AA), Southwest Airlines (WN), and United Airlines (UA) each told CBS that none of their in-service 737 MAX aircraft use the affected software. Southwest told CNBC that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes." Those statements concern aircraft already in service. For new deliveries, Southwest and United have told Boeing they will not accept delivery of new aircraft with the affected software and would take aircraft with a previous version instead, CBS reported. The fleet statements cover four U.S. carriers. CBS said it had also contacted Allegiant Air (G4), which operates the 737 MAX, for comment. Boeing told Airways it did not have specific aircraft figures to share, so it remains unclear how many undelivered aircraft carry versions 14 or 14.1, or whether any operator outside the U.S. already flies with them. An airline first told Boeing about the condition in November 2024, according to CBS. Boeing reviewed it and concluded in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue. Boeing received what a source described to CBS as "additional information from operators" earlier this year, which prompted it to launch a formal safety review board. The Wall Street Journal reported that the formal review began in September, according to an Investing.com summary of the newspaper's report . The board's findings went to the FAA this month and will be reviewed by the CARB. Boeing told Airways that it informed the FAA of the issue as part of its safety review process and is working under the agency's oversight to complete the software update. The FAA certified the 737-7 on August 3. CBS reported that the aircraft was certified with software version 14 and that Southwest, which accounts for nearly all of the type's order book, had been set to begin receiving it this fall; it is unclear whether the airline will take delivery now. CNBC reported it was not immediately clear whether the 737-7 could be delivered or flown with an older software version. The 737-10 used version 14.1 during its certification testing, according to CBS. Boeing completed the final planned certification flight in July, and Alaska Chief Operating Officer Jason Berry told Reuters on September 24 that the airline expected FAA certification by the end of September . Aviation Week reported that it remains unclear whether the software issue will affect the timing of either 737-7 deliveries or 737-10 certification. The FAA's statement did not address either program. Alaska said on September 26 that it has been engaged with Boeing and the FAA "and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps." Alaska holds an order for 105 737-10s and options for 35 more . In his September 24 interview, before the software issue was reported, Berry said Alaska expected its first aircraft in spring 2027 and passenger service between April and mid-May that year. He added that Alaska must complete certification work on the pilots' head-up display after the FAA approves the aircraft, a process he expected to take a "few months." The CARB will review Boeing's safety findings, and the FAA told Airways that the board will also review Boeing's proposed solution. Boeing told Airways it had no further information at this time on whether 737-7 deliveries can proceed with an earlier software load, whether the fix will require pilot training beyond a software update, or what additional operator information prompted its formal safety review. The FAA's statement to Airways did not say whether the CARB must conclude before the agency certifies the 737-10. Following a thorough review, a panel of FAA safety experts on Friday determined a software issue in certain Boeing 737 MAX flight computers is not a safety concern. The FAA’s Corrective Action Review Board made that determination because pilots retain full control of the aircraft and the indications to the flight crew are clear and unambiguous. In a statement to Airways, a Boeing spokesperson said the company informed all 737 operators last month "about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario" and "shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases." The spokesperson said Boeing's engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the problem.
The FAA's statement did not address either program.
Alaska said on September 26 that it has been engaged with Boeing and the FAA "and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps."

Boeing told Airways it had no further information at this time on whether 737-7 deliveries can proceed with an earlier software load, whether the fix will require pilot training beyond a software update, or what additional operator information prompted its formal safety review.

Boeing completed the final planned certification flight in July, and Alaska Chief Operating Officer Jason Berry told Reuters on September 24 that the airline expected FAA certification by the end of September .
Alaska holds an order for 105 737-10s and options for 35 more .
In his September 24 interview, before the software issue was reported, Berry said Alaska expected its first aircraft in spring 2027 and passenger service between April and mid-May that year.
He added that Alaska must complete certification work on the pilots' head-up display after the FAA approves the aircraft, a process he expected to take a "few months."
CBS reported that Boeing's initial bulletin also said updated pilot guidance would follow in November, and that Boeing is working to bring both forward.
The fleet statements cover four U.S. carriers.
CBS said it had also contacted Allegiant Air (G4), which operates the 737 MAX, for comment.
Southwest told CNBC that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes."

In that situation, the flight guidance system may incorrectly transition out of vertical navigation (VNAV) to a simpler pitch mode such as level change or vertical speed, according to Boeing's description of the problem reported by Aviation Week .
Boeing reviewed it and concluded in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue.

CBS noted the scenario would typically occur close to the airport, where crew workload is already high, and Boeing said pilots must take additional steps to use automated guidance on the next approach.

sources.title: Meta Open Sources Muse Gadgets, Lets Developers Build Their Own Hardware For Its AI Agent - officechai.com
passages: Nat Friedman, who leads product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, has announced Muse Gadgets, an open source ESP32 firmware and Linux SDK that lets anyone build hardware devices that work with the company’s personal AI agent .
Meta has manufactured a batch of 5,000 Home Links, which Friedman says should be ready to ship in a few weeks.
They are free for Muse subscribers while supplies last.
According to the Gadgets site, the offer is limited to subscribers in the United States, with one per subscriber, and claiming a unit only holds a place in line rather than placing an order.
All of the code for Home Link is open source too.
Developers can grab an API token from the Muse Gadgets site and point their coding agent of choice at the GitHub repository to start building peripherals.
Muse launched on September 8 as Meta’s first consumer-facing agentic app, and has since added commerce tie-ups with Shopify, PayPal, Instacart and Expedia.
Friedman has also acknowledged that Muse was heavily inspired by OpenClaw, the open source agent created by Peter Steinberger, who later joined OpenAI .
Meta is taking some big bets with its AI agent, Muse.
Meta says community-built skills could let Muse turn on a light, control a TV or send a document to a printer, depending on a user’s setup.
Opening up the hardware side follows a similar playbook to OpenClaw’s: put the code in the hands of tinkerers and see what they come up with.
Muse Gadgets is available at gadgets.muse.ai, and the SDK is on GitHub at facebookincubator/muse-gadget-sdk.

extraction.body: Meta is taking some big bets with its AI agent, Muse. Meta now wants Muse to leave the screen. Nat Friedman, who leads product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, has announced Muse Gadgets, an open source ESP32 firmware and Linux SDK that lets anyone build hardware devices that work with the company’s personal AI agent . Developers can grab an API token from the Muse Gadgets site and point their coding agent of choice at the GitHub repository to start building peripherals. The code is released under the Apache 2.0 license. The ESP32 SDK is aimed at off-the-shelf microcontroller boards. Builders can add a screen to show images, audio in and out, or other sensors. The Linux SDK, meanwhile, turns a spare Raspberry Pi or other Linux machine into a Muse gadget, with custom commands that can let Muse handle sysadmin chores or work with a Home Assistant setup. Meta has listed a number of project ideas to get people started. One is a round AMOLED touchscreen from Waveshare, which comes with push-to-talk, a speaker, a microphone and a battery. Another is Seeed’s reTerminal E1002, a colour e-ink display that could show a morning briefing, reminders or a shopping list. M5Stack’s pocket-sized StickS3 shows Muse’s status on a colour screen, while the AiPi Lite is a small desk companion that answers out loud and shows pictures. Home Assistant’s Voice Preview Edition, meanwhile, pairs push-to-talk with an LED ring that shows Muse’s status. An HDMI stick that would let Muse put content on a TV screen is listed as coming soon. Meta also runs a community Discord where builders can share projects, and says it may feature the best ones on the Gadgets site. Meta has also built a gadget of its own. Muse Home Link is a small USB-C powered device that connects Muse to a user’s home network, so the agent can talk to smart home devices such as TVs and speakers, and to anything else that exposes an HTTP interface. Meta says community-built skills could let Muse turn on a light, control a TV or send a document to a printer, depending on a user’s setup. Meta has manufactured a batch of 5,000 Home Links, which Friedman says should be ready to ship in a few weeks. They are free for Muse subscribers while supplies last. According to the Gadgets site, the offer is limited to subscribers in the United States, with one per subscriber, and claiming a unit only holds a place in line rather than placing an order. All of the code for Home Link is open source too. The move extends a product that has had a busy few weeks. Muse launched on September 8 as Meta’s first consumer-facing agentic app, and has since added commerce tie-ups with Shopify, PayPal, Instacart and Expedia. It has also drawn comparisons with OpenAI’s rival agents, to the point that OpenAI’s CFO mistakenly called her company’s new Dots agents “Muse” in a TV interview. Friedman has also acknowledged that Muse was heavily inspired by OpenClaw, the open source agent created by Peter Steinberger, who later joined OpenAI . Opening up the hardware side follows a similar playbook to OpenClaw’s: put the code in the hands of tinkerers and see what they come up with. The Gadgets site is upfront that this is a hacker project, warning that side effects of tinkering may include bricked boards and voided warranties. Muse Gadgets is available at gadgets.muse.ai, and the SDK is on GitHub at facebookincubator/muse-gadget-sdk.

passages: And just now, Meta has announced a new move: officially launching the Muse Gadgets open source project to fully delegate hardware capabilities, enabling global makers and developers to build exclusive peripheral hardware devices for Muse.
In response to everyone's curiosity about why Meta took the open source move, Alexandr Wang said, "First of all, building all kinds of small gadgets is fun in itself.

According to the information released by Meta, developers can use the ESP32 development board to run the Muse firmware, or use the Linux SDK to connect more complex devices, which means that developers can not only deploy the Muse interaction logic on low-cost microcontrollers, but also directly run the Muse client on more powerful edge computing devices such as Raspberry Pi 5.
For developers who want to get started and try it out, you can follow the steps below to start building your own exclusive Muse peripheral right now:

We believe that Muse is at a special moment, it provides unlimited possibilities for people to create new types of hardware devices, and we are very much looking forward to seeing what kind of works everyone will end up building!"
Meta's route may be exactly this: Muse is responsible for the intelligent capabilities, and developers are responsible for creating various carriers.
In the future, Muse may exist in smartphones, smart glasses, various home devices, and even new hardware created by developers...

extraction.body: Meta's Muse is still gaining continuous momentum. This newly launched personal AI Agent has already become a key product in Meta's AI strategy this year. Different from traditional chatbots, Muse is designed as an intelligent assistant that can perform tasks on behalf of users: processing emails, shopping, planning itineraries, and even completing a number of complex operations continuously in the background. And just now, Meta has announced a new move: officially launching the Muse Gadgets open source project to fully delegate hardware capabilities, enabling global makers and developers to build exclusive peripheral hardware devices for Muse. According to the information released by Meta, developers can use the ESP32 development board to run the Muse firmware, or use the Linux SDK to connect more complex devices, which means that developers can not only deploy the Muse interaction logic on low-cost microcontrollers, but also directly run the Muse client on more powerful edge computing devices such as Raspberry Pi 5. The official side has also listed a variety of highly practical DIY form references: HDMI Display Stick / Large Screen Expansion: Project the interface or interaction of the Muse Agent directly to a TV or external monitor. Touch-controlled Handheld Pendant: Make a portable interactive terminal similar to Muse Charm, so that you can talk to the Agent at any time without wearing smart glasses. For developers who want to get started and try it out, you can follow the steps below to start building your own exclusive Muse peripheral right now: At the same time, Meta has also launched an official device: Muse Home Link, a small USB-C powered device, which allows Muse to connect to your home network to communicate with smart home devices, such as TVs, speakers, and any devices that support HTTPS interfaces, further bringing the AI Agent into real life scenarios. The official stated that 5000 units of Muse Home Link have been produced in the first trial production run, and shipments are expected to start in a few weeks. While stocks are sufficient, the devices will be distributed directly for free to eligible Muse subscription users for experience. In response to everyone's curiosity about why Meta took the open source move, Alexandr Wang said, "First of all, building all kinds of small gadgets is fun in itself. Secondly, we hope to unlock the creativity of developers and let everyone explore all kinds of brand new, even crazy ideas. We believe that Muse is at a special moment, it provides unlimited possibilities for people to create new types of hardware devices, and we are very much looking forward to seeing what kind of works everyone will end up building!" From this perspective, Meta seems to hope that Muse is not just an official product, but an extensible platform. As soon as the project was released, it immediately attracted the attention of netizens, and even some netizens got started and DIYed their own Muse devices. There are many more user cases like this. Through this attempt of Muse, we can also see a change in the Agent era: In the past, the development path of smart hardware was usually: Company designs hardware — Users purchase devices — Develop applications. But AI Agent may move towards another model: The company provides models and Agent capabilities — Developers create devices of various forms. In fact, starting from AI Pin, the industry has made a lot of explorations in AI hardware, and has tried to replace the mobile phone entry through independent devices, but many products are affected by problems such as functional restrictions and poor interactive experience. Now, manufacturers seem to be changing their minds: directly build a powerful AI Agent first, and then let it enter different hardware. Meta's route may be exactly this: Muse is responsible for the intelligent capabilities, and developers are responsible for creating various carriers. In the future, Muse may exist in smartphones, smart glasses, various home devices, and even new hardware created by developers... So what about you, what do you think of Meta's this attempt? coreStoryFacts.text: Meta now lets you make your own Muse gadgets that feature the company’s new AI agent with code that the company open sourced.
“Muse gadgets are open source devices you build yourself,” Meta says.
With the Muse Home Link, you use community-built skills to have the AI agent “turn on a light, control your TV, send a document to a printer, and more, depending on your setup,” Meta says.

Nat Friedman, who leads product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, has announced Muse Gadgets, an open source ESP32 firmware and Linux SDK that lets anyone build hardware devices that work with the company’s personal AI agent .
Meta has manufactured a batch of 5,000 Home Links, which Friedman says should be ready to ship in a few weeks.
They are free for Muse subscribers while supplies last.
According to the Gadgets site, the offer is limited to subscribers in the United States, with one per subscriber, and claiming a unit only holds a place in line rather than placing an order.
All of the code for Home Link is open source too.
Developers can grab an API token from the Muse Gadgets site and point their coding agent of choice at the GitHub repository to start building peripherals.
Muse launched on September 8 as Meta’s first consumer-facing agentic app, and has since added commerce tie-ups with Shopify, PayPal, Instacart and Expedia.
Friedman has also acknowledged that Muse was heavily inspired by OpenClaw, the open source agent created by Peter Steinberger, who later joined OpenAI .
Meta is taking some big bets with its AI agent, Muse.
Meta says community-built skills could let Muse turn on a light, control a TV or send a document to a printer, depending on a user’s setup.
Opening up the hardware side follows a similar playbook to OpenClaw’s: put the code in the hands of tinkerers and see what they come up with.
Muse Gadgets is available at gadgets.muse.ai, and the SDK is on GitHub at facebookincubator/muse-gadget-sdk.

And just now, Meta has announced a new move: officially launching the Muse Gadgets open source project to fully delegate hardware capabilities, enabling global makers and developers to build exclusive peripheral hardware devices for Muse.
In response to everyone's curiosity about why Meta took the open source move, Alexandr Wang said, "First of all, building all kinds of small gadgets is fun in itself.

According to the information released by Meta, developers can use the ESP32 development board to run the Muse firmware, or use the Linux SDK to connect more complex devices, which means that developers can not only deploy the Muse interaction logic on low-cost microcontrollers, but also directly run the Muse client on more powerful edge computing devices such as Raspberry Pi 5.
For developers who want to get started and try it out, you can follow the steps below to start building your own exclusive Muse peripheral right now:

We believe that Muse is at a special moment, it provides unlimited possibilities for people to create new types of hardware devices, and we are very much looking forward to seeing what kind of works everyone will end up building!"
Meta's route may be exactly this: Muse is responsible for the intelligent capabilities, and developers are responsible for creating various carriers.
In the future, Muse may exist in smartphones, smart glasses, various home devices, and even new hardware created by developers...

At the same time, Meta has also launched an official device: Muse Home Link, a small USB-C powered device, which allows Muse to connect to your home network to communicate with smart home devices, such as TVs, speakers, and any devices that support HTTPS interfaces, further bringing the AI Agent into real life scenarios.
It described Muse Gadgets as open-source devices you build yourself.

sources.title: Meta Open-Sources Muse Gadgets: Empower Global Developers to Independently Build Custom AI Peripherals - 36Kr
passages: And just now, Meta has announced a new move: officially launching the Muse Gadgets open source project to fully delegate hardware capabilities, enabling global makers and developers to build exclusive peripheral hardware devices for Muse.
In response to everyone's curiosity about why Meta took the open source move, Alexandr Wang said, "First of all, building all kinds of small gadgets is fun in itself.

According to the information released by Meta, developers can use the ESP32 development board to run the Muse firmware, or use the Linux SDK to connect more complex devices, which means that developers can not only deploy the Muse interaction logic on low-cost microcontrollers, but also directly run the Muse client on more powerful edge computing devices such as Raspberry Pi 5.
For developers who want to get started and try it out, you can follow the steps below to start building your own exclusive Muse peripheral right now:

We believe that Muse is at a special moment, it provides unlimited possibilities for people to create new types of hardware devices, and we are very much looking forward to seeing what kind of works everyone will end up building!"
Meta's route may be exactly this: Muse is responsible for the intelligent capabilities, and developers are responsible for creating various carriers.
In the future, Muse may exist in smartphones, smart glasses, various home devices, and even new hardware created by developers...

At the same time, Meta has also launched an official device: Muse Home Link, a small USB-C powered device, which allows Muse to connect to your home network to communicate with smart home devices, such as TVs, speakers, and any devices that support HTTPS interfaces, further bringing the AI Agent into real life scenarios.

extraction.body: Meta's Muse is still gaining continuous momentum. This newly launched personal AI Agent has already become a key product in Meta's AI strategy this year. Different from traditional chatbots, Muse is designed as an intelligent assistant that can perform tasks on behalf of users: processing emails, shopping, planning itineraries, and even completing a number of complex operations continuously in the background. And just now, Meta has announced a new move: officially launching the Muse Gadgets open source project to fully delegate hardware capabilities, enabling global makers and developers to build exclusive peripheral hardware devices for Muse. According to the information released by Meta, developers can use the ESP32 development board to run the Muse firmware, or use the Linux SDK to connect more complex devices, which means that developers can not only deploy the Muse interaction logic on low-cost microcontrollers, but also directly run the Muse client on more powerful edge computing devices such as Raspberry Pi 5. The official side has also listed a variety of highly practical DIY form references: HDMI Display Stick / Large Screen Expansion: Project the interface or interaction of the Muse Agent directly to a TV or external monitor. Touch-controlled Handheld Pendant: Make a portable interactive terminal similar to Muse Charm, so that you can talk to the Agent at any time without wearing smart glasses. For developers who want to get started and try it out, you can follow the steps below to start building your own exclusive Muse peripheral right now: At the same time, Meta has also launched an official device: Muse Home Link, a small USB-C powered device, which allows Muse to connect to your home network to communicate with smart home devices, such as TVs, speakers, and any devices that support HTTPS interfaces, further bringing the AI Agent into real life scenarios. The official stated that 5000 units of Muse Home Link have been produced in the first trial production run, and shipments are expected to start in a few weeks. While stocks are sufficient, the devices will be distributed directly for free to eligible Muse subscription users for experience. In response to everyone's curiosity about why Meta took the open source move, Alexandr Wang said, "First of all, building all kinds of small gadgets is fun in itself. Secondly, we hope to unlock the creativity of developers and let everyone explore all kinds of brand new, even crazy ideas. We believe that Muse is at a special moment, it provides unlimited possibilities for people to create new types of hardware devices, and we are very much looking forward to seeing what kind of works everyone will end up building!" From this perspective, Meta seems to hope that Muse is not just an official product, but an extensible platform. Now, manufacturers seem to be changing their minds: directly build a powerful AI Agent first, and then let it enter different hardware. Ten Injured in Australia as Car Crashes into Crowd North of Sydney Ten people were injured when a man drove into a crowd in the Australian city of Newcastle on Saturday after appearing to lose control of the car, authorities said. The 18-year-old driver was ‌arrested at ‌the scene in ‌the suburb ⁠of Wallsend about ⁠110 km (70 miles) north of the New South Wales state capital, Sydney. When the incident occurred, fans had lined local streets to send ⁠off the Newcastle ‌Knights rugby ‌league team, due to compete in ‌the country's National Rugby ‌League grand final in Sydney on Sunday. Two of those hospitalized, a 5-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man, ‌were in a critical condition, authorities said. Newcastle Mayor ⁠Gavin ⁠Morris said the driver seemed to have lost control of the car. "It appears that he was revving the car in some form," Morris said in televised remarks. Police said initial indications suggested the incident was not terrorism-related. Russia Strikes Another Major Bridge in Ukraine Capital A Russian strike targeted a major bridge in Kyiv, its mayor said Saturday, in another attack on Ukrainian infrastructure that has brought traffic chaos to the capital. The attack on the Northern Bridge, which followed a drone alert, came a day after the Southern Bridge was hit in a wave of strikes that city officials say is "tearing Kyiv apart". The grinding conflict, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, has largely focused on ground fighting in the east, with Kyiv mostly spared from the devastation wrought near the frontline, AFP said. "Northern Bridge has been hit," Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram on Saturday. "Emergency services are heading to the scene." In another update, Klitschko said the attack had damaged the road surface and trolleybus wires on the bridge. "Traffic across the bridge from the left bank to the right bank is currently blocked," Klitschko said. The latest strike follows multiple attacks on crossings over the Dnipro river that link the eastern and western parts of the capital. The Southern Bridge is one of eight crossings connecting the two sides of Kyiv. The cable-stayed structure had already been hit several times since Thursday, according to city officials. Klitschko warned Friday the capital should now be on a war footing. Siavash Jamshidi was accused of targeting security personnel during mass demonstrations that peaked in January in which thousands of people were killed, said AFP. Since that time, Iranian authorities have stepped up executions of convicts linked to the unrest. "Jamshidi was sentenced to death on charges of moharebeh through brandishing and firing a firearm, as well as conspiracy and collusion against national security," Iran's judiciary said, using the legal term moharebeh to mean "waging war against God". The judiciary's Mizan Online website said he was also found guilty of offences not related to the protests, including "fraud, making threats, theft, possession and carrying of an illegal military-grade weapon". Other charges included "complicity in kidnapping, brandishing a weapon to intimidate, and intentional infliction of bodily harm". Mizan said Jamshidi was "active" during the demonstrations, which were sparked in December last year by grievances over living costs in Iran, but peaked on January 8 and 9 with huge rallies. Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths in the unrest, attributing the violence to "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel. Foreign-based NGOs however maintain that Iranian security forces fired on protesters. US President Donald Trump threatened at the time to intervene militarily in Iran. Weeks later in late February, the United States and Israel launched a joint attack on the Iranian republic, triggering the Middle East war.

CNN, CBS and Axios reported Trump is set to name the director of national intelligence (DNI) as his pick for so-called “AI tsar”. The decision could be announced as early as Friday. Amid increasing calls for the government to intervene in the rapidly developing technology, Trump last month announced on social media that he would be naming a new AI tsar. “Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” he wrote. Trump already had one AI tsar, venture capitalist David Sacks. He resigned earlier this year and became an external adviser to the president. Clayton, who previously served as the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York and chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, was confirmed by the US Senate in July to oversee the nation’s spy agencies. He succeeded Bill Pulte, a controversial Trump loyalist who was appointed by the president as acting director of the US intelligence community. It’s unclear whether Clayton would hold the role of AI tsar in addition to his duties as DNI. “Any personnel announcement will be announced directly by the President. Any reporting until then is baseless speculation,” a White House official told Al Jazeera. Clayton’s possible selection comes on the heels of warnings from multiple AI researchers that the technology could kill humans within a decade. It also comes as AI giant Anthropic prepares for what is expected to be a blockbuster initial public offering (IPO), aimed for next month, and has warned that US government attitudes towards the company could impact its business. According to an IPO prospectus seen by the Reuters news agency, the AI company said the Trump administration’s attacks and lawsuits on its technology could hurt relationships with customers and other government partners. The filing also revealed that AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”. A federal appeals court ruled last week that the US government could blacklist Anthropic from US Department of Defense contracts. The court said that the agency “had ample support for its conclusion” that the company’s products pose a supply chain risk to the Pentagon and its contractors due to code that prevents them from performing certain tasks. Anthropic has said it will not allow its technology to be used for autonomous weapons or surveillance. Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei and Clayton attended Tuesday’s AI meeting at the White House. Ten Injured in Australia as Car Crashes into Crowd North of Sydney Ten people were injured when a man drove into a crowd in the Australian city of Newcastle on Saturday after appearing to lose control of the car, authorities said. The 18-year-old driver was ‌arrested at ‌the scene in ‌the suburb ⁠of Wallsend about ⁠110 km (70 miles) north of the New South Wales state capital, Sydney. When the incident occurred, fans had lined local streets to send ⁠off the Newcastle ‌Knights rugby ‌league team, due to compete in ‌the country's National Rugby ‌League grand final in Sydney on Sunday. Two of those hospitalized, a 5-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man, ‌were in a critical condition, authorities said. Newcastle Mayor ⁠Gavin ⁠Morris said the driver seemed to have lost control of the car. "It appears that he was revving the car in some form," Morris said in televised remarks. Since that time, Iranian authorities have stepped up executions of convicts linked to the unrest. "Jamshidi was sentenced to death on charges of moharebeh through brandishing and firing a firearm, as well as conspiracy and collusion against national security," Iran's judiciary said, using the legal term moharebeh to mean "waging war against God". The judiciary's Mizan Online website said he was also found guilty of offences not related to the protests, including "fraud, making threats, theft, possession and carrying of an illegal military-grade weapon". Other charges included "complicity in kidnapping, brandishing a weapon to intimidate, and intentional infliction of bodily harm". Mizan said Jamshidi was "active" during the demonstrations, which were sparked in December last year by grievances over living costs in Iran, but peaked on January 8 and 9 with huge rallies. Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths in the unrest, attributing the violence to "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel. Foreign-based NGOs however maintain that Iranian security forces fired on protesters. US President Donald Trump threatened at the time to intervene militarily in Iran. Weeks later in late February, the United States and Israel launched a joint attack on the Iranian republic, triggering the Middle East war.

sources.title: Trump to name intelligence chief Jay Clayton as AI tsar: Reports - Al Jazeera
passages: United States President Donald Trump is expected to select spy chief Jay Clayton to oversee development of the nation’s artificial intelligence industry, according to multiple news reports.
CNN, CBS and Axios reported Trump is set to name the director of national intelligence (DNI) as his pick for so-called “AI tsar”.
The decision could be announced as early as Friday.
Amid increasing calls for the government to intervene in the rapidly developing technology, Trump last month announced on social media that he would be naming a new AI tsar.
“Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” he wrote.
Trump already had one AI tsar, venture capitalist David Sacks.
He resigned earlier this year and became an external adviser to the president.
“Any personnel announcement will be announced directly by the President.
Any reporting until then is baseless speculation,” a White House official told Al Jazeera.

According to an IPO prospectus seen by the Reuters news agency, the AI company said the Trump administration’s attacks and lawsuits on its technology could hurt relationships with customers and other government partners.
The filing also revealed that AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”.
It’s unclear whether Clayton would hold the role of AI tsar in addition to his duties as DNI.
Last month, Trump lashed out at Amodei over his plea for an AI slowdown, calling fears of the technology a “hoax” and a “scam”.
Trump also blasted the public backlash to data centres.

extraction.body: United States President Donald Trump is expected to select spy chief Jay Clayton to oversee development of the nation’s artificial intelligence industry, according to multiple news reports. CNN, CBS and Axios reported Trump is set to name the director of national intelligence (DNI) as his pick for so-called “AI tsar”. The decision could be announced as early as Friday. Amid increasing calls for the government to intervene in the rapidly developing technology, Trump last month announced on social media that he would be naming a new AI tsar. “Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” he wrote. Trump already had one AI tsar, venture capitalist David Sacks. He resigned earlier this year and became an external adviser to the president. Clayton, who previously served as the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York and chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, was confirmed by the US Senate in July to oversee the nation’s spy agencies. He succeeded Bill Pulte, a controversial Trump loyalist who was appointed by the president as acting director of the US intelligence community. It’s unclear whether Clayton would hold the role of AI tsar in addition to his duties as DNI. “Any personnel announcement will be announced directly by the President. Any reporting until then is baseless speculation,” a White House official told Al Jazeera. Clayton’s possible selection comes on the heels of warnings from multiple AI researchers that the technology could kill humans within a decade. It also comes as AI giant Anthropic prepares for what is expected to be a blockbuster initial public offering (IPO), aimed for next month, and has warned that US government attitudes towards the company could impact its business. According to an IPO prospectus seen by the Reuters news agency, the AI company said the Trump administration’s attacks and lawsuits on its technology could hurt relationships with customers and other government partners. The filing also revealed that AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”. A federal appeals court ruled last week that the US government could blacklist Anthropic from US Department of Defense contracts. The court said that the agency “had ample support for its conclusion” that the company’s products pose a supply chain risk to the Pentagon and its contractors due to code that prevents them from performing certain tasks. Anthropic has said it will not allow its technology to be used for autonomous weapons or surveillance. Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei and Clayton attended Tuesday’s AI meeting at the White House. Clayton was also a guest at last month’s White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping. Last month, Trump lashed out at Amodei over his plea for an AI slowdown, calling fears of the technology a “hoax” and a “scam”. Trump also blasted the public backlash to data centres. Amid the public pushback against the facilities, Amazon announced on Friday that it is investing $1bn over the next five years into US communities where it operates them. Matt Garman, the CEO of the company’s cloud computing business, wrote in a blog post that the money would go towards education, job training, water preservation projects and other local priorities.

passages: If you want to invest in a crypto exchange-traded fund (ETF) with room to run, there are a few options that should be at the top of your list, like the Bitwise Solana Staking ETF ( BSOL -0.12% ) , the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF ( IBIT -0.48% ) , and the iShares Ethereum Trust ETF ( ETHA -1.28% ) .
Let's first establish why these three funds have significant upside potential at this moment in particular, and then take a look at what you'd be getting with each.

As of Sept. 29, Bitcoin was 33% below its $126,080 all-time high, Ethereum is 46% below its $4,946 peak, and Solana was about 60% below its record high of $293. All three of these records were set in 2025.
Not one of these three coins is priced at a hype premium right now. If anything, they have plenty of room to run before they start to look overheated.
The ETFs that hold them are therefore positioned to experience a lot of inflows, provided that the factors that drove their relatively recent run-ups, or new drivers, are in play.
The Bitcoin fund's $66.8 billion in net assets makes up a lion's share of the $107.8 billion held by all U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs as of Sept. 30.

During the crypto bear market , in the period from Dec. 31, 2025, to June 30, 2026, its net assets fell by 36%. Its shares outstanding (which correspond to the fund units that investors hold) fell by just 4.6%. In other words, prices changed for the worse, but most holders stayed. By Sept. 30, the share count had climbed to above June's total, right as its cumulative net inflows reached $65 billion.
The Ethereum ETF has flightier holders. Its shares outstanding declined by 22% in the first half of 2026, then jumped 36% by Sept. 28.

The Ethereum ETF doesn't offer staking (locking coins in exchange for a trickle of new coins). Its sibling, the iShares Staked Ethereum Trust ETF , does have staking, with 30-day rewards of 1.35%. Keep in mind that the IRS counts staking rewards as taxable income in the year you receive them.

The Solana ETF is the only one of the three funds that pays a yield, with a 5.5% net reward rate. So far, it has drawn in an overwhelming proportion of all cumulative net capital inflows to U.S. spot Solana funds. But one of the important details here is that its yield will likely shrink.

In August 2026, Solana stakers approved the governance measure called SIMD-0550, which speeds up the decline in new coin issuance over the long term. After its activation, which will likely occur in early 2027, the baseline reward rate will decline from 5.8% to about 4.3% within a year, and then reach a rate of 2.2% in about 2029.
With issuance bottoming at 1.5% a year, most of that yield will go to preventing your slice of Solana from being diluted so much. But there isn't really any Solana ETF that does this any better.
If you were to split $1,000 across these three crypto ETFs , a good move is to put $600 into the Bitcoin fund, with the Solana and Ethereum ETFs splitting the rest evenly.

The fact that the Bitcoin fund's holders seem willing to retain their shares through downturns in Bitcoin's price is nice, but the real reason it deserves the larger weighting is that Bitcoin itself is probably the safest major cryptocurrency to invest in, and it won't be going anywhere. Ethereum and Solana, although strong players, both need to compete against myriad rivals to succeed, and over the very long term, they might lose, so their allocation needs to be smaller.

ASX exchange traded funds ( ETFs ) can be a simple way to get exposure to long-term trends without having to pick every individual winner yourself. It also gives investors exposure to the physical side of automation. Factories, warehouses, hospitals, logistics networks, and manufacturers are all looking for ways to become more efficient. Robotics and automation can help with labour shortages, productivity, safety, and precision. That gives the fund a long runway if more businesses keep investing in machines, sensors, chips, and intelligent systems. Another ASX ETF that could be worth a closer look is the Betashares Video Games and Esports ETF. This fund invests in global companies linked to video games and interactive entertainment. Its holdings include NetEase ( NASDAQ: NTES ), Take-Two Interactive ( NASDAQ: TTWO ), and Nintendo ( FRA: NTO ). Nintendo is a useful example of the type of business this fund can own. It has some of the world's most recognisable gaming franchises, a loyal customer base, and a history of creating hardware and software ecosystems that keep players engaged. A third ASX ETF to consider is the Betashares Global Quality Leaders ETF. This fund focuses on global companies with strong quality characteristics. Rather than targeting one specific theme, the fund looks for companies with strong financial profiles, including profitability, balance sheet strength, cash generation, and earnings stability.
